title: 10-Year Sealed-Battery Smoke and CO Alarms With Voice Alerts: Two Options Compared
subtitle: How talking combination alarms can protect a parent's home from fire and carbon monoxide for about a decade, and what they still cannot do.
excerpt: A sealed 10-year battery means no battery swaps, and a voice that says "Fire" is clearer than a beep. Here are two options to compare, how many alarms a home needs, and the limits to know.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most of us know the sound: a single chirp at 2 a.m. from a smoke alarm that wants a new battery. For an older parent, answering that chirp can mean reaching up to the ceiling in the dark, which is a chore nobody enjoys.

A 10-year sealed-battery alarm is built to skip that chore. Kidde describes its battery as a sealed lithium battery, and First Alert describes its own as a 10-year sealed battery. Choose a combination model that senses both smoke and carbon monoxide (CO), add a voice that says what is wrong, and one device covers two dangers with words instead of just beeps.

Both alarms here are photoelectric-based combination units. Kidde says its alarm has photoelectric and electrochemical sensors. The makers point out that photoelectric alarms sense smoldering fires sooner, while ionization alarms sense fast flames sooner. When the alarm sounds, a recorded voice names the problem. The Kidde says "Fire" or "Warning, Carbon Monoxide," and its page says the voice also covers a low battery. The First Alert voice tells you the type and location of the danger.

A sealed battery cannot be recharged or swapped. First Alert says its alarm gives low-battery chirps for the life of the alarm and an end-of-life warning, and Kidde says its alarm chirps at the end of its life. After about 10 years, the whole unit goes in the trash. The U.S. Fire Administration says to replace the whole alarm 10 years from its manufacture date.

It helps to know the limits, too. These are standalone alarms. They do not call family or the fire department, and two or more single alarms are not interconnected (interconnected alarms all sound together). If one goes off in the kitchen, a parent asleep far from it may not hear it. They also have no strobe light or bed shaker. FEMA says people with significant hearing loss need a separate specialty alarm. These alarms also do not suit someone who needs remote alerts while away.

items: Count before you shop. FEMA recommends an alarm in every bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level of the home, basement included. A 3-bedroom home needs several alarms, plus CO coverage on each level.
Compare the price per alarm, not per box. The Kidde price is for a 2-pack, and the First Alert price is for one alarm. Neither alarm here has a monthly fee.
Check the manufacture date printed on the alarm. One that sat on a shelf has less than 10 years of life left.
Look for a single test/silence button. Both alarms here have one.
Choose a voice that names the danger. A spoken "Fire" is clearer than beeps alone, especially for someone waking up groggy.
Consider fewer cooking false alarms. First Alert lists Precision Detection technology to reduce cooking nuisance alarms.
Check the warranty and return terms with the seller. First Alert lists a 10-year limited warranty; we could not confirm Kidde's.

sections.content: Both alarms are smoke-and-CO combinations with no monthly fee. The First Alert page states it conforms to UL 217 10th Edition and UL 2034. Prices are as published in October 2026: Kidde is $64.50 per alarm in the 2-pack, and First Alert is $69.99 per alarm, so check current price at each seller before you decide. We could not confirm Kidde's sound level or dimensions.
Setting them up and using them well

The Kidde alarm turns itself on when it is attached to its mounting bracket, with no pull-tabs or switches. With the First Alert alarm, you choose from 11 pre-programmed home locations, so pick the one that matches where that alarm will go and the voice will announce it.
Reaching the ceiling to install an alarm, or to press the test button each month, can be risky on a ladder. Plan for a helper for both jobs.
"Test smoke alarms every month." — U.S. Fire Administration

If the home already has hardwired alarms, which have a backup battery that needs yearly replacement, or has an older-home setup, an electrician may be needed. A voice can help someone understand the danger, but it cannot tell a parent what to do next, so the family still needs a plan for getting out. FEMA also suggests keeping bedroom doors closed at night to slow smoke and fire.

If your parent is deaf or severely hard of hearing, a voice alarm is not suitable. FEMA says a person with significant hearing loss needs a separate specialty alarm; ask their audiologist which type fits.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A sealed-battery voice alarm will not do everything, but it removes a common battery chore and swaps confusing beeps for a plain warning. Count the rooms, compare the per-alarm prices, and then mark your calendar twice: once for the monthly test, and once for the replacement date 10 years after the manufacture date.
